title: Of the Incomparable Virtues of Patience
summary: On the third day, the Third Wazir argued that persistent patience is often mistaken for weakness: 'Sire, he who waits too long allows his enemies to build fortresses around him;...
full_text:
On the third day, the Third Wazir argued that persistent patience is often mistaken for weakness: 'Sire, he who waits too long allows his enemies to build fortresses around him; action must be swift and uncompromising!'

Bakhtiyar stepped forward and delivered his counter-discourse on the majesty of patience:

'O King, let not the hasty confuse patience with sluggish weakness! Impatience is the fire of the straw, which blazes furiously for a second and leaves only cold black ash; but patience is the deep, steady heat of the furnace that tempers the finest Damascus steel.

Patience is the virtue by which the tiny acorn becomes the mighty oak that defies the storms of a century; it is the quality by which the silkworm weaves its cocoon, and the diamond crystal is forged in the darkness of the earth.

He who possesses patience can smile at insults, knowing that truth requires no loud shout to defend itself; he can endure the winter of misfortune, knowing that spring is already walking across the hills.

The impatient man breaks his bow by bending it with violent haste; but the patient archer waits until the breath is still and the aim is true, hitting the mark of honor, even as the history of Abu Sabir demonstrates across all generations.'
moral: Patience under trial is an unshakeable shield; it disarms wrath and turns the bitterest cup into sweet nectar.
